newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch BNG eyes new investors in Yankee market.
newsitem.headline: Dutch BNG eyes new investors in Yankee market.

text.p: Bank Nederlandse Gemeenten (BNG), the most active Dutch issuer in international capital markets, said on Wednesday it planned to expand issuance in Japan and tap the U.S. domestic market for the first time.
In an interview, executives said BNG, jointly owned by the Dutch state and municipalities, aimed to broaden its investor base by issuing non-guilder bonds away from the Dutch market.
"We are considering, in the long term, the U.S. market," senior vice-president Treasury, Bert de Kock, told Reuters.
This would continue the process begun in 1993 when BNG started diversifying its funding base.
The proportion of borrowings in currencies other than guilders has risen to 65 percent this year from nil before 1993.
The AAA-rated bank raised the equivalent of 11.87 billion guilders on global markets in calendar 1995 and to date in 1996 has raised 10 billion for its local government customers.
It has not yet issued into the Yankee market although it has issued dollar-denominated Eurobonds since 1993.
De Kock said U.S. investor interest in European issuers should rise with the introduction of the Euro currency in 1999.
But he said BNG may tap the U.S. domestic market before then in a bid to establish its name.
Bart van Dooren, BNG's head of international funding, said borrowers had to issue into the Yankee market once or twice a year to offer investors the liquidity.
"You have to make sure it makes sense to go for U.S. registration," he said.
Of BNG's 26 issues this year, six have been in yen, with two Samurai issues targeted at Japanese retail investors.
De Kock said BNG may issue another one or two Samurai bonds in 1997.
"Japan is potentially a very big market where we could raise more money than we have already done," he said.
About five percent of its funds raised since 1993 have been in yen, although the proportion in 1996 is 12.7 percent.
But van Doorsen said this figure could reach 20 percent.
"There are a lot of institutions. It takes some time to have your name established there (in Japan)," he said.
De Kock said the advent of the single European currency would create a huge, liquid bond market for borrowers like BNG.
"Our appetite for going to the market could increase when the Euro materialises," he said, adding BNG aimed to be one of the "top names" among European borrowers.

He also said BNG may issue only another one billion guilders of bonds this year because it has raised so much earlier in the year when swap opportunities were more attractive and demand from its customers was weaker.
"We have stored some cheap money," he said.
BNG could afford to maintain its aggressive targets for borrowing costs because it did not need much more money if the targets were not met.
Van Dooren said the 1997 borrowing task would be about the same as 1996, but this would depend on demand.
The proportion of funds borrowed in guilders was higher in 1995 at 68 percent compared with 35 percent this year because the guilder was strong.
With the guilder more stable this year, many investors were looking to the higher yields available on German debt than Dutch bonds.
De Kock said BNG may redeem some bonds early, particularly higher-coupon paper maturing between 1998 and 2003.
